questions.q: What defines "cloud computing" as opposed to traditional on-premises IT?
options: Cloud computing means running software only on a single physical server you own
On-demand access to computing resources (compute, storage, networking) over the internet, provisioned and billed dynamically rather than owning and maintaining physical hardware
Cloud computing requires no internet connection whatsoever
Cloud computing is just a marketing term with no technical distinction from on-prem
questions.explain: Cloud computing's defining traits are on-demand self-service provisioning and consumption-based billing over the internet, replacing the need to buy, house, and maintain physical servers yourself.

questions.q: What's the difference between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS?
options: IaaS gives you raw infrastructure (VMs, networking) you manage yourself; PaaS gives you a managed platform to deploy code onto without managing the underlying servers; SaaS delivers a complete, ready-to-use application
They are three names for the same thing
IaaS is only for databases, PaaS only for storage, and SaaS only for VMs
SaaS requires you to manage the operating system yourself
questions.explain: These three models sit on a spectrum of how much the provider manages for you: IaaS hands you infrastructure and you handle the OS up, PaaS handles the OS and runtime so you focus on your app, and SaaS is a finished application you simply use.

questions.q: What is an Azure Availability Zone?
options: A synonym for an Azure region
A billing tier with no physical meaning
A physically separate location within an Azure region, with independent power, cooling, and networking, used to protect applications from datacenter-level failures
A type of virtual network only
questions.explain: Availability Zones are physically distinct datacenter groupings within a region, each with its own power and cooling, so a failure affecting one zone (a power outage, for example) is far less likely to affect the others.

questions.q: What's the relationship between an Azure region and an Azure Availability Zone?
options: A region is a smaller subset of a single Availability Zone
An Availability Zone is a geographic area containing many regions
A region is a geographic area containing datacenters; some regions further divide into multiple Availability Zones for higher resilience
They are unrelated concepts with no connection to each other
questions.explain: A region is the broader geographic footprint (e.g. East US), and within many regions, Microsoft further separates datacenters into Availability Zones so resources can be spread across zones for higher resilience within that same region.

questions.q: What is an Azure subscription?
options: A single virtual machine
A synonym for a resource group
A type of storage account
A billing and access-management boundary that contains resources and is linked to an Azure AD/Entra tenant, defining what you're billed for and who can manage what
questions.explain: A subscription is the top-level container tying resource usage to billing and to an identity tenant. Resource groups and the resources within them live inside a subscription, not the other way around.

questions.q: What is a resource group used for in Azure?
options: A physical datacenter
A logical container that groups related resources (e.g. a VM, its disk, its network) for unified lifecycle management, access control, and billing organization
A single subscription's entire set of regions
A backup mechanism only
questions.explain: A resource group is purely a management construct — it has no physical location of its own — that lets you deploy, monitor, secure, and delete a related set of resources together as one unit.

questions.q: What's the difference between an Azure VM and Azure App Service for hosting a web application?
options: They are identical products marketed under different names
App Service requires you to manually configure the OS just like a VM does
VMs cannot be used to host web applications

A VM gives full control over the OS and everything installed on it, requiring you to manage patching and scaling yourself; App Service is a managed PaaS for hosting web apps where Azure handles the underlying OS and much of the scaling
questions.explain: A VM is IaaS: you own the OS, patching, and scaling decisions. App Service is PaaS purpose-built for web apps — you deploy code, and Azure manages the underlying compute, OS patching, and much of the scaling for you.

questions.q: What is Azure Blob Storage primarily designed for?
options: Storing large amounts of unstructured data (files, images, backups, logs) accessed via a REST API
Structured relational data with enforced schemas
Running virtual machines directly
Hosting DNS records
questions.explain: Blob storage is object storage optimized for large volumes of unstructured data — files, media, backups, logs — accessed over HTTP/HTTPS via a REST API, rather than a relational, schema-enforced store.

questions.q: What is a Virtual Network (VNet) in Azure used for?
options: A backup service for storage accounts
A pricing tier for compute resources
A private network within Azure where you can control IP address ranges, subnets, and connectivity for your resources, similar to a traditional on-prem network
A synonym for a resource group
questions.explain: A VNet is your own isolated network space inside Azure, letting you define address ranges, subnets, routing, and connectivity rules for the resources placed inside it, much like a network you'd design on-premises.

questions.q: What does Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) primarily provide?
options: A billing dashboard only
Identity and access management — authenticating users and applications and controlling what they can access across Azure and other connected services
A type of virtual machine
A content delivery network
questions.explain: Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity platform: it authenticates users and applications and, combined with RBAC, governs what they're authorized to do across Azure resources and other integrated apps.

questions.q: What does Azure Monitor collect and let you do?
options: It collects metrics and logs from Azure resources, letting you set up alerts, dashboards, and diagnose performance or availability issues
It is only a static, unchangeable status page
It replaces the need for any resource configuration
It only monitors on-premises servers, never Azure resources
questions.explain: Azure Monitor centralizes telemetry — metrics and logs — from Azure resources (and can ingest from on-prem/hybrid sources too), and provides alerting and dashboarding on top of that data to catch problems proactively.

questions.q: Why would you configure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) at the resource group level rather than granting access to each resource individually?
options: RBAC only works at the subscription level, never at resource groups
RBAC cannot be scoped to a resource group at all
Resource-group-level RBAC disables all individual resource permissions
RBAC assignments at a resource group scope apply to everything inside it, simplifying permission management instead of assigning roles resource-by-resource
questions.explain: RBAC role assignments are inherited down the scope hierarchy (management group, subscription, resource group, resource), so assigning a role at the resource group level automatically applies it to every resource inside, cutting down repetitive per-resource assignments.

questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege in the context of Azure IAM?
options: Granting every user Owner access by default for convenience
Granting users and applications only the permissions they actually need to do their job, and nothing more
Removing all access controls to simplify management
Giving all users the same single role regardless of function
questions.explain: Least privilege minimizes the blast radius of a compromised or mistaken account by ensuring identities hold only the specific permissions their role requires, rather than broad access that's rarely all needed.

questions.q: What's a key tool for controlling and forecasting Azure spending?
options: Azure Cost Management + Billing, which tracks spend, forecasts costs, and can set budgets with alerts
There is no way to track Azure spending until the invoice arrives
Azure Monitor is the only tool for cost tracking
Resource groups automatically cap spending on their own
questions.explain: Cost Management + Billing gives visibility into current and historical spend, cost forecasts, and budget alerts, letting teams catch runaway costs before the monthly invoice rather than being surprised by it.

questions.q: What does an Azure Policy do?
options: It is identical to an RBAC role assignment
It only applies to storage accounts
It enforces organizational rules on resources (e.g. "only allow VMs in these regions" or "require a specific tag"), auditing or blocking non-compliant resources
It replaces the need for management groups
questions.explain: Azure Policy is a governance tool separate from RBAC: RBAC controls who can do what, while Policy controls what configurations are allowed at all, evaluating and optionally blocking or flagging resources that don't comply with defined rules.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Azure Management Groups?
options: A billing feature with no access-control implications
A synonym for a resource group
A tool exclusively for tagging resources
Organizing multiple subscriptions under a hierarchy so policies and RBAC can be applied consistently across many subscriptions at once
questions.explain: Management groups sit above subscriptions in Azure's scope hierarchy, letting an organization apply a single policy or role assignment across many subscriptions at once rather than configuring each subscription separately.

questions.q: What is the Azure CLI primarily used for?
options: A GUI-only tool that cannot be scripted
A command-line tool for creating, managing, and scripting Azure resources, usable across Windows, macOS, and Linux
A billing report generator
A tool exclusively for Azure AD, unrelated to resource management
questions.explain: The Azure CLI is a cross-platform command-line tool for managing Azure resources, making it well suited to automation and scripting in a way the Portal's point-and-click interface isn't.

questions.q: What is an ARM template?
options: A JSON file that declaratively defines the Azure resources to deploy and their configuration, processed by Azure Resource Manager
A binary executable for Azure VMs
A type of virtual network
A pricing calculator
questions.explain: ARM templates describe the desired end state of your infrastructure in JSON. Azure Resource Manager reads that declarative definition and reconciles real infrastructure to match it — the same underlying mechanism Bicep compiles down to.

questions.q: When you deploy your first resource through the Azure Portal, what underlying service actually processes and creates it?
options: The Azure CLI, and only the Azure CLI
A third-party deployment tool entirely outside of Azure
The resource group's tag list
Azure Resource Manager (ARM), the deployment and management layer that all Azure interfaces — Portal, CLI, ARM templates, Bicep, SDKs — ultimately go through
questions.explain: Every management surface in Azure, including the Portal itself, ultimately submits requests through Azure Resource Manager, which is the consistent control plane that authenticates the request, applies policy, and provisions the resource.

questions.q: What does the AZ-900 certification exam primarily test?
options: Deep, hands-on Kubernetes administration skills
Advanced Azure Kubernetes Service networking configuration
Foundational knowledge of cloud concepts, core Azure services, and Azure pricing, support, and governance basics
Only Azure DevOps pipeline configuration
questions.explain: AZ-900 (Microsoft Azure Fundamentals) is an entry-level exam covering broad conceptual knowledge — what cloud computing is, Azure's core service categories, and pricing/support/governance basics — rather than deep hands-on skill with any one service.
